key_terms.meaning: A nonempty set S together with a binary operation ∗ that is closed (a∗b ∈ S) and associative: (a∗b)∗c = a∗(b∗c).
A semigroup that also has an identity element e, with e∗a = a∗e = a for every a.
The element e of a monoid such that e∗a = a∗e = a; for addition it is 0, for multiplication it is 1.
A monoid in which every element a has an inverse a⁻¹ with a∗a⁻¹ = a⁻¹∗a = e.
For a in a group, the unique element a⁻¹ such that a∗a⁻¹ = e; under addition it is written −a.
|G|, the number of elements in the group G.
A nonempty subset H of a group G that is itself a group under the same operation; written H ≤ G.
A group G in which some element g gives every element as a power: G = ⟨g⟩ = {gⁿ : n ∈ ℤ}.
An element g with G = ⟨g⟩; a cyclic group of order n has φ(n) generators.
The group of all n! permutations of {1, 2, …, n} under composition of functions.
Every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the permutation group of its own elements.
For H ≤ G and a ∈ G, the left coset aH = {a∗h : h ∈ H}; left cosets are disjoint and all have |H| elements.
[G : H], the number of distinct left cosets of H in G; for finite G it equals |G| ÷ |H|.
If H ≤ G and G is finite, then |H| divides |G|, so |G| = [G : H] × |H|.
H ≤ G with g∗h∗g⁻¹ ∈ H for all h ∈ H and all g ∈ G; written H ⊲ G, and then aH = Ha for every a.
A map φ : G → G′ with φ(a∗b) = φ(a)∗′φ(b) for all a, b ∈ G; it carries e to e′ and inverses to inverses.
ker φ = {g ∈ G : φ(g) = e′}, always a normal subgroup of G; φ is one-one exactly when ker φ = {e}.
Repeated division: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, r) where a = qb + r, 0 ≤ r < b, until the remainder is 0.
a ≡ b (mod n) means n divides a − b; it splits ℤ into n residue classes [0], [1], …, [n−1].
If n₁, …, n_k are pairwise coprime, the system x ≡ a_i (mod n_i) has exactly one solution modulo n₁n₂⋯n_k.

takeaways: A semigroup only needs closure and associativity; adding an identity gives a monoid, and adding inverses too gives a group.
Groups describe symmetry: every group is a set of reversible actions that can be composed and undone.
A cyclic group is the simplest group — one element builds everything, and ℤₙ under addition is the standard model.
Cayley's theorem removes the mystery from abstract groups: each one is just a group of permutations in disguise.
Cosets cut a group into equal disjoint blocks, and that is exactly why Lagrange's theorem works.
Lagrange's theorem gives a fast test: a subset of size that does not divide |G| can never be a subgroup.
Normal subgroups are the ones whose cosets can be multiplied together, so they are the ones that give quotient groups.
The Euclidean algorithm finds gcd(a, b) in very few steps, and the same steps give the integers x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b).
Congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation, so modular arithmetic works with classes instead of numbers.
The Chinese remainder theorem turns one hard congruence modulo a big number into several easy ones modulo coprime factors.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually ask for a full proof — closure and associativity checked term by term, a coset or subgroup computation shown in full, or a Euclidean-algorithm run with every division written out.

bank.q: Define a binary operation, a semigroup, a monoid and a group. Give one example of each, and one example of a semigroup that is not a monoid.
outline: Binary operation on S is a map S × S → S, written a∗b
Semigroup: closure plus associativity (a∗b)∗c = a∗(b∗c)
Monoid: semigroup plus identity e with e∗a = a∗e = a
Group: monoid plus inverse a⁻¹ for every element
Examples: positive integers under addition form a semigroup but have no identity, so not a monoid; (ℕ₀, +) is a monoid but not a group; (ℤ, +) is a group

bank.q: State Lagrange's theorem. Using it, prove that in a finite group the order of every element divides the order of the group.
outline: Statement: if H ≤ G and |G| is finite then |H| divides |G|
The order of an element a is the order of the cyclic subgroup ⟨a⟩
⟨a⟩ is a subgroup, so its order divides |G| by Lagrange
Conclude a^|G| = e for every a, with proof of why a^k = e exactly for multiples of the order

bank.q: State and prove Cayley's theorem, and write down the permutation of the four elements of ℤ₄ given by addition of 1.
outline: Statement: every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the permutation group on the set G
For each a ∈ G define the map φ_a : G → G by φ_a(x) = a∗x
Show φ_a is a bijection: injective from left cancellation, surjective because x = a∗(a⁻¹∗x)
Show the map a ↦ φ_a is a homomorphism and has trivial kernel
Example: on ℤ₄, adding 1 gives the 4-cycle (0 1 2 3)

bank.q: Define a normal subgroup and a group homomorphism. Prove that the kernel of a group homomorphism is a normal subgroup.
outline: Definitions of normal subgroup (g h g⁻¹ ∈ H) and of homomorphism φ(a∗b) = φ(a)∗′φ(b)
ker φ is nonempty because φ(e) = e′
Closure: φ(a∗b⁻¹) = φ(a)∗′(φ(b))⁻¹ = e′, so ab⁻¹ ∈ ker φ
Normality: φ(g h g⁻¹) = φ(g)e′φ(g)⁻¹ = e′ for h ∈ ker φ
Hence ker φ ⊲ G, and φ is one-one iff ker φ = {e}

bank.q: Use the Euclidean algorithm to find gcd(1001, 429) and write it in the form 1001a + 429b. State the value of a and b.
outline: Back-substitute: 143 = 1001 − 2·429
Check: 143 divides both numbers and no larger common divisor exists
Answer a = 1, b = −2

bank.q: List all subgroups of ℤ₁₂ and, for H = {0, 4, 8}, write all cosets in ℤ₁₂. Verify Lagrange's theorem for this H.
outline: Subgroups correspond to divisors of 12: orders 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12
⟨4⟩ = {0, 4, 8} has order 3
The four cosets are disjoint and cover ℤ₁₂
Index is 4 = 12 ÷ 3, matching Lagrange's theorem

bank.q: Find all solutions of the simultaneous congruences x ≡ 1 (mod 3), x ≡ 2 (mod 5), x ≡ 3 (mod 7) using the Chinese remainder theorem.
outline: Moduli 3, 5, 7 are pairwise coprime, so a unique solution exists modulo 105
Build x = 1·M₁·y₁ + 2·M₂·y₂ + 3·M₃·y₃ with M₁ = 35, M₂ = 21, M₃ = 15
Find the inverses: y₁ = 2 (35·2 ≡ 1 mod 3), y₂ = 1 (21 ≡ 1 mod 5), y₃ = 1 (15 ≡ 1 mod 7)
Verify 52 satisfies all three congruences

bank.q: Show that the set of units modulo 9 forms a group under multiplication modulo 9, find the order of each element, and decide whether the group is cyclic.
outline: Units U(9) = {1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8}; an element is a unit iff gcd(a, 9) = 1
Closure, associativity inherited from ℤ, identity 1, each element self-inverse or paired: 2·5 ≡ 1, 4·7 ≡ 1, 8·8 ≡ 1
Orders: 1 has order 1; 8 has order 2; 2, 4, 5, 7 have order 6
Powers of 2: 2, 4, 8, 7, 5, 1, so ⟨2⟩ = U(9) and the group is cyclic
Number of generators is φ(6) = 2, namely 2 and 5

bank.q: Prove that congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation on ℤ, list the residue classes modulo 5, and find the inverse of 3 modulo 7.
outline: Reflexive: n divides a − a; symmetric: sign change; transitive: n divides the sum of two multiples of n
Classes: [0], [1], [2], [3], [4], each an infinite arithmetic progression with common difference 5
The classes are disjoint and cover ℤ
Inverse of 3 mod 7: solve 3x ≡ 1 (mod 7), giving x ≡ 5 since 15 ≡ 1
The inverse exists because gcd(3, 7) = 1

bank.q: Prove that every group of prime order is cyclic, and classify all groups of order 4 up to isomorphism.
outline: Take a ≠ e in G of prime order p; the subgroup ⟨a⟩ has order dividing p and greater than 1, so it is p
Hence G = ⟨a⟩ and G ≅ ℤ_p
For order 4: if some element has order 4 the group is ℤ₄
Otherwise every non-identity element has order 2, so the group is abelian and is the Klein four-group V₄
ℤ₄ and V₄ are not isomorphic because ℤ₄ has an element of order 3? — no: because ℤ₄ has an element of order 4 and V₄ has none

bank.q: Let H be a subgroup of G. Prove that H is normal if and only if every left coset of H equals the corresponding right coset, and use this to build the quotient group ℤ/nℤ.
outline: H normal means g h g⁻¹ ∈ H for all g, h
This is equivalent to gH ⊆ Hg, and applying it to g⁻¹ gives the reverse inclusion
Coset multiplication (aH)(bH) = abH is well defined exactly when H is normal; check it does not depend on representatives
In the abelian group ℤ every subgroup nℤ is normal, so the cosets form ℤ/nℤ
ℤ/nℤ has n elements and addition is carried out modulo n

bank.q: Prove that every finite cyclic group of order n is isomorphic to ℤₙ under addition, and count the generators of ℤ₁₂.
outline: Let G = ⟨a⟩ with aⁿ = e; define φ : ℤₙ → G by φ(k) = aᵏ
φ is well defined because aᵏ depends only on k mod n
φ is a homomorphism: φ(j + k) = a^{j+k} = aʲaᵏ
φ is onto by definition of cyclic and one-one because the powers a⁰, …, a^{n−1} are distinct
Generators of ℤ₁₂ are the classes coprime to 12: 1, 5, 7, 11, so φ(12) = 4

bank.q: State the fundamental theorem of arithmetic. Use it to find gcd(720, 1350) and lcm(720, 1350), then compare the work with the Euclidean algorithm.
outline: Statement: every integer greater than 1 is a product of primes, unique up to order
gcd takes the smaller exponent of each prime: 2 · 3² · 5 = 90
lcm takes the larger exponent: 2⁴ · 3³ · 5² = 10800
Check gcd × lcm = 720 × 1350; the Euclidean algorithm needs no factorisation and is faster for large numbers

bank.q: Using Lagrange's theorem, prove Fermat's little theorem, and apply it to compute 3¹⁰⁰ mod 7.
outline: The nonzero classes modulo p form a group of order p − 1 under multiplication
The class of a has order dividing p − 1, so a^{p−1} ≡ 1 (mod p) when p does not divide a
For p = 7: 3⁶ ≡ 1 (mod 7)
Check the exponent reduction is valid because the powers repeat with period dividing 6

glossary.def: A rule that assigns to each ordered pair (a, b) of elements of a set S exactly one element a∗b of S.
A property of a subset or set: applying the operation to two members always gives a member of the same set.
The law (a∗b)∗c = a∗(b∗c), which lets us drop brackets when combining three or more elements.
A set with a closed associative binary operation.
A semigroup with an identity element.
A set with an associative operation, an identity, and an inverse for each element.
A group in which a∗b = b∗a for all elements; named after Niels Henrik Abel.
The smallest positive integer k with aᵏ = e; it equals the order of the subgroup ⟨a⟩.
A nonempty subset H of a group G closed under the operation and under taking inverses.
A group in which every element is a power of a single element.
A bijection from a finite set to itself, usually written in two-line or cycle notation.
The group Sₙ of all permutations of n symbols under composition, with order n!.
A translate aH = {a∗h : h ∈ H} or Ha = {h∗a : h ∈ H} of a subgroup H.
The number [G : H] of distinct cosets of H in G.
A subgroup H with gHg⁻¹ = H for every g in G, so that its cosets form a group.
G/H, the group of cosets of a normal subgroup H, with multiplication (aH)(bH) = abH.
A map between groups that preserves the operation: φ(a∗b) = φ(a)∗′φ(b).
A bijective homomorphism; two groups related by one are structurally the same.
The set of elements a homomorphism sends to the identity; it measures how far the map is from being one-one.
a divides b, written a | b, when b = ak for some integer k.
gcd(a, b) is the largest positive integer dividing both a and b; it is 1 when a and b are coprime.
For integers a and b there exist integers x and y with ax + by = gcd(a, b).
The set [a] = {a + kn : k ∈ ℤ} of all integers congruent to a modulo n.
A system of congruences with pairwise coprime moduli has a unique solution modulo the product of the moduli.
